title: Guard the mind (35–39)
hookLine: hard to see, subtle, going where it likes: a guarded mind brings happiness

lines: COULD YOU GUARD JUST ONE THING?
cards: A young man has just become a monk. He's sincere. Then his teachers start on the rules: how to wear the robe, how to eat, how to walk into a village, what is allowed, what is not.
Rule after rule. His heart sinks. He can't possibly keep all that; maybe he should go back to lay life after all.
He's brought to the Buddha, ready to give up. And the Buddha asks him a surprisingly simple question: could you guard just one thing?

teach.b: In the commentary's story, the young man says yes, he could guard one thing. Then guard your mind, the Buddha says, and you won't need to worry about the rest. And he speaks verse thirty-six.
Müller's English describes thoughts as “difficult to perceive, very artful,” rushing wherever they like, and it ends: “thoughts well guarded bring happiness.”

teach.h: HARD TO SEE, GOING WHERE IT LIKES.
teach.b: Verse thirty-five says the same with a different verb: the mind is hard to hold and flighty, and “a tamed mind brings happiness.”
Verse thirty-seven adds that it travels far, moves alone, has no body, and hides in the cave of the heart. That's not an insult. It's an honest field guide.
You can't guard something you haven't looked at. Guarding here doesn't mean locking the mind in a box, or fighting every thought.
The Pali word is closer to protecting, keeping watch, the way a gatekeeper watches who comes in. Thoughts will come; the guard notices them at the gate. This one can come in.
That one, the old resentment, the spiral of worry, maybe not today.

Verses thirty-eight and thirty-nine finish the chapter's middle: wisdom can't grow in a mind that's always unsteady, and the one whose mind is watched and calm has nothing to fear. There's a real kindness in the story.
The young man's problem wasn't lack of goodness. It was overwhelm. And the answer wasn't a longer list.
It was one thing, done well: watch the gate.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes sum up the discipline as guarding the mind, and meditators practice noting where attention wanders and gently returning it.

o: let one guard: keep watch over the mind like a gate
fight off every thought the moment it appears
lock the mind away so no thoughts can get in

games.q: match the pieces of verses thirty-five to thirty-nine.
p: guard just one thing: the mind
the mind hides in the cave of the heart

s: guarding the mind means fighting and stopping every thought
it's closer to a gatekeeper: noticing what comes in, not locking the mind away.
verse thirty-seven says the mind travels far, moves alone and has no body
and it hides in the cave of the heart.
in the commentary, the Buddha gave the overwhelmed young man a longer list of rules
he gave him one thing to guard: his mind.

games.q: you're a new monk, and the rules overwhelm you. you're about to give up. what does the Buddha say in the story?
o: then this life isn't for you.
could you guard just one thing? then guard your mind.
games.why: the Buddha shrank the task to one thing: guard the mind. then he spoke verse thirty-six.

practice: Make the breath your gatekeeper's post, and just watch where the mind goes: off to a memory, a plan, a song. Each time, name it softly, “planning,” “remembering,” and come back to the post.
You're not stopping it from going, only learning its routes, the places it likes to wander.

wordCard.voice: Rakkhetha. Let one guard: the mind, hard to see, subtle, going where it likes, watched like a gate, brings happiness when guarded.

orig.note: Pali: let one guard, from verse thirty-six: 'cittam rakkhetha medhavi,' let the wise guard the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: watch the gate. Not a longer list: one thing, guarded well. Day one hundred sixty-six.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 37–39; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of a discontented monk (verse 36)
